en: Vibhaṅga:
Analysis of the Factors of the Path 1.
Suttantabhājanīya (The Exposition according to the Discourses)
The Noble Eightfold Path, namely:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In this context, what is right view?
Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering—
this is called right view.
In this context, what is right intention?
The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of non-cruelty—
this is called right intention.
In that regard, what is right speech?
Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter—
this is called right speech.
In this context, what is right action?
Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct—
this is called right action.
In this context, what is right livelihood?
Here, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, maintains his life by right livelihood—
this is called "right livelihood.
In this context, what is right effort?
Here, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states;
he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states;
he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states.

One generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen—
this is called right effort (*sammāvāyāma*).
In this context, what is right mindfulness (*sammāsati*)?
Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world—
this is called right mindfulness.
In this context, what is right concentration?

Here, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
And with the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body;
That which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous"— entering and abiding in this third jhāna;

and with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, entering and abiding in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity—
this is called right concentration.
The Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In this context, what is right view?
Here, a bhikkhu develops right view dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment;
he develops right intention … [and so on] … he develops right speech … [and so on].
He develops right action …pe… he develops right livelihood …pe… he develops right effort …pe…
He develops right mindfulness …pe… he develops right concentration,
which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
This is the Exposition according to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya).
2. Analysis according to the Abhidhamma:
The Eightfold Path—right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In this regard, what is the eightfold path?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation and results in the diminution [of defilements], for the abandoning of views and for the attainment of the first stage—secluded from sensual pleasures... [and so forth]... having attained the first jhāna.
He dwells in a practice that is painful with sluggish direct knowledge; at that time there is the eightfold path:
right view …pe… right concentration.
In this context, what is right view?

That which is wisdom, understanding … [as above] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view, the factor of enlightenment consisting in the investigation of phenomena, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called "right view.
In this context, what is right intention?

Whatever is thought, initial thought, intention, absorption, sustained absorption, the directing of the mind, right intention, a factor of the path, included within the path— this is called "right intention.
In this context, what is right speech?

That which is the refraining, abstaining, desisting, and abstinence from the four types of verbal misconduct; the non-doing, non-performing, non-transgression, non-overstepping of the limit, and the destruction of the bridge [to such conduct]; right speech that is a factor of the path and included within the path—this is called "right speech.
In this context, what is right action?

That which is the refraining from, the abstaining from, the desisting from, the abstinence from, the non-doing of, the non-performing of, the non-transgression of, the not overstepping the limit of, and the destruction of the bridge regarding the three types of bodily misconduct; right action that is a factor of the path and included within the path—this is called “right action.
In this context, what is right livelihood?

That which is the absence of delight in, the abstaining from, the refraining from, the desisting from, the non-performance, the non-doing, the non-transgression, the not overstepping the limit, the destruction of the bridge [of misconduct], right livelihood, a factor of the path,
included within the path— this is called "right livelihood.
In this context, what is right effort?
That which is the mental arousal of energy … [as above] … right effort, the factor of enlightenment of energy, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called "right effort.
In this context, what is right mindfulness?
That mindfulness which is recollection … [as before] … right mindfulness, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called “right mindfulness.
In this context, what is right concentration?
That stability of the mind … [as before] … right concentration, the concentration enlightenment factor, a path factor included in the path—
this is called “right concentration.
This is called “the eightfold path.”
The remaining phenomena are associated with the eightfold path.
The fivefold path consists of:
right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In this regard, what is the five-factored path?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, conduces to the waning of existence, and results in the abandoning of views for the attainment of the first stage—secluded from sensual pleasures... [and so on] ...he enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna.
He dwells in a practice that is painful with sluggish direct knowledge; at that time, there is a five-factored path:
right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In this context, what is right view?

That which is wisdom, understanding … [as above] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view, the factor of enlightenment consisting of investigation of phenomena, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called "right view.
In this context, what is right intention?
Whatever thought, applied thought … [and so on] … right intention, which is a factor of the path and included within the path—
this is called “right intention.
In this context, what is right effort?
That which is the mental arousal of energy … [as above] … right effort, the factor of enlightenment of energy, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called "right effort.
In this context, what is right mindfulness?
That mindfulness which is recollection … [as before] … right mindfulness, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called “right mindfulness.
In this context, what is right concentration?
That stability of the mind … right concentration, which is the concentration enlightenment factor, a path factor, included in the path—
this is called "right concentration.
This is called "the five-factored path."
The remaining phenomena are associated with the five-factored path.
The five-factored path consists of:
right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In this context, what is right view?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, conduces to the waning of existence, and results in the abandoning of views for the attainment of the first stage—secluded from sensual pleasures... [and so on]... having attained the first jhāna.
He dwells in a practice that is painful with sluggish direct knowledge; at that time, whatever wisdom there is, understanding … pe … non-delusion,
investigation of phenomena, right view, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, a factor of the path included in the path— this is called "right view."

The remaining phenomena are associated with right view … [and so on] … the remaining phenomena are associated with right intention … [and so on] … the remaining phenomena are associated with right effort … [and so on].
The remaining factors are associated with right mindfulness.
In this context, what is right concentration?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation and conducive to the destruction of the acquisitions, [freeing him] from views...
For the sake of abandoning [the hindrances] and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures...
he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge; at that time, whatever stability of mind there is...
right concentration, the concentration enlightenment factor, the path factor, included in the path—this is [right concentration].
This is called "right concentration.
The remaining factors are associated with right concentration.
This is the eightfold path.
Right view ... pe ... right concentration.
In this context, what is the eightfold path?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation and results in the dismantling of the acquisitions of views.
For the sake of abandoning [the hindrances] and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge; at that time there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.

Through having performed and cultivated that very same supramundane wholesome jhāna, he, secluded from sensual pleasures … pe … enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice, slow in its direct knowledge, and empty;

at that time, there is the eightfold path: 1. Right view 2. Right intention 3. Right speech 4. Right action 5. Right livelihood 6. Right effort 7. Right mindfulness 8. Right concentration At that time, these eight factors constitute the path.
Right view …pe… right concentration.
This is called the "eightfold path.
All remaining phenomena are associated with the eightfold path.
The five-factored path:
right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In this context, what is the five-factored path?

Here, monks, at whatever time a monk develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, conduces to the waning of existence, and results in the abandoning of views, for the attainment of the first stage—being secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in its direct knowledge—at that time there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
As the result of having performed and cultivated that very same supramundane wholesome jhāna, secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice, slow in its direct knowledge, and empty.
At that time, there is a five-factored path:
right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
This is called "the five-factored path."
The remaining phenomena are associated with the five-factored path.
The five-factored path consists of:
right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In this context, what is right view?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, conduces to the waning of existence, and results in the abandoning of views for the attainment of the first stage—being secluded from sensual pleasures... [and so forth] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
He dwells in a practice that is painful and slow in direct knowledge; at that time there is contact …pe… there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
Through the performance and development of that very same supramundane wholesome jhāna, [there arises] the result, secluded from sense pleasures …pe…
... pe ... he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge, and is empty;

whatever at that time is wisdom, understanding, ... pe ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view, the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, a factor of the path, included within the path—this is that.
This is called "right view.
The remaining states are associated with right view...
[and so on] ...the remaining states are associated with right intention... [and so on].
The remaining phenomena are associated with right effort … [and so on] … the remaining phenomena are associated with right mindfulness.
In this context, what is right concentration?

Here, bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, which leads to the destruction [of the taints], for the abandoning of views, for the attainment of the first stage—secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...having entered upon the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge—at that time there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
As a result of having performed and cultivated that very same supramundane wholesome jhāna, he—
quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as before] … enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice, slow in its higher knowledge, and empty.
Whatever at that time is the steadiness, stability, firmness, non-wavering, non-distraction, state of mental non-distraction, serenity, the faculty of concentration,
the power of concentration, right concentration, the concentration factor of enlightenment, the path factor, and that which is included in the path—
this is called "right concentration."
The remaining states are associated with right concentration.
This concludes the Exposition according to the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya). 3.
The Interrogation (Pañhāpucchaka).
The Noble Eightfold Path, namely:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Of these eight path factors, how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate? … [and so on] … how many are with conflict, and how many are without conflict?
3.1. The Triplet.
It may be wholesome, it may be indeterminate.
Right intention associated with pleasant feeling;
The seven path factors may be associated with pleasant feeling, or they may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
They may be resultants, or they may be states tending toward resultancy.
They are not acquired through clinging and are not conducive to clinging.
They are undefiled and not subject to defilement.
Right intention is without initial application and with sustained application only;

the seven path factors may be with both initial and sustained application, may be without initial application and with sustained application only, or may be without both initial and sustained application.
Right intention is accompanied by rapture, accompanied by pleasure, and not accompanied by equanimity.
Seven path-factors may be accompanied by rapture, may be accompanied by pleasure, or may be accompanied by equanimity.
They are not to be abandoned either by seeing or by cultivation.
They have roots that are to be abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation.
They may be conducive to diminution; they may be neither conducive to accumulation nor conducive to diminution.
They may be of those in training (sekha); they may be of those beyond training (asekha).
Immeasurable.
Having an immeasurable object.
Exalted.
It may be fixed in rightness, or it may be unfixed.
It does not have the Path as its object; it may have the Path as its cause, or it may have the Path as its predominance;
or it may be so that it cannot be said to "have the Path as its cause" nor "have the Path as its predominance."
They may have arisen, they may not have arisen, or they may be in the process of arising.
They may be past, they may be future, or they may be present.
They should not be described as having a past object, nor as having a future object, nor as having a present object.
They may be internal, they may be external, or they may be both internal and external.
They have external objects.
They are non-manifesting and non-reactive.
3.2. 3.2 Duka 3.2.1. Hetugocchaka:
Right view is a cause; the seven path factors are not causes; they are accompanied by a cause; they are associated with a cause.

Right view is both a cause and accompanied by a cause; the seven path factors should not be said to be "both causes and accompanied by causes," but rather they are "accompanied by causes and are not causes.

Right view is both a cause and associated with a cause; the seven path factors should not be said to be "both causes and associated with causes," but rather they are "associated with causes and are not causes.

The seven path factors are not causes but are accompanied by causes; right view should not be said to be "not a cause but accompanied by a cause," nor should it be said to be "not a cause and unaccompanied by a cause."
3.2.2. The Minor Intermediate Dyads:
With Conditions;
Conditioned.
Non-indicative.
Non-reactive.
Formless.
Supramundane.
Cognizable by some, not cognizable by others.
3.2.3. The Group on Taints (Āsava-gocchaka).
Without taints.
Untainted. Dissociated from taints.
They should not be described as "both taints and associated with taints," nor as "associated with taints but not taints.
They should not be described as "both taints and associated with taints," nor as "associated with taints but not taints.
They are dissociated from taints.
They are without taints.
11.3.2.4. The Group on Fetters, etc.:
They are not fetters … [and so on] …
There are no fetters … [and so on] … no floods … [and so on] … no yokes … [and so on] …
There are no hindrances …pe… no misapprehensions …pe…. 3.2.10.
The Greater Pair (Mahantaraduka)
Possessing an object;
not mind;
mental factors.
Associated with consciousness.
Conjoined with consciousness.
Generated by consciousness.
Co-existent with consciousness;
following after consciousness;
conjoined with, and produced by, consciousness.
Conjoined with, originated by, and co-existent with the mind;
conjoined with, originated by, and following after the mind;
external.
Neither grasping nor grasped. 11.3.2.11.
The Section on Grasping (Upādāna-gocchaka), etc.
There are no clinging-aggregates … [and so on] … there are no defilements … [and so on] … they are not to be abandoned by vision.
Not to be abandoned by cultivation.
Not having as their cause that which is to be abandoned by vision.
Not having as their cause that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.
Right intention is without applied thought (*avitakka*); seven factors of the path may be with applied thought, or they may be without applied thought.
Right intention is accompanied by sustained thought (*savicāra*); seven factors of the path may be with sustained thought, or they may be without sustained thought.
Right intention is accompanied by rapture (*sappītika*); seven factors of the path may be accompanied by rapture, or they may be without rapture.
Right intention accompanied by rapture: seven factors of the path may be accompanied by rapture, or they may not be accompanied by rapture.
Right intention accompanied by pleasure: seven factors of the path may be accompanied by pleasure, or they may not be accompanied by pleasure.
Right intention is not accompanied by equanimity; seven factors of the path may be accompanied by equanimity, or they may not be accompanied by equanimity.
Neither belonging to the sense sphere,
nor belonging to the fine-material sphere,
nor belonging to the immaterial sphere.
They are not included within the mundane.
They may be leading to liberation, or they may not lead to liberation.
They may be fixed, or they may be unfixed.
The Unsurpassed.
Non-conflict.
The Interrogation on Questions.
The Analysis of the Factors of the Path is finished.
